title: Dumbbell Lunge
overview: The dumbbell lunge targets the quadriceps, hamstrings, glutes, and calves while also engaging the core for stability.This exercise is a unilateral movement, meaning it primarily works one leg at a time. By challenging each leg independently, it improves lower body strength, balance, and coordination. It also mimics functional movements, improving flexibility andmobilityin the hips and legs.The lunge is a foundational movement pattern that should be incorporated into everyworkout programand trained fairly frequently.Those looking to add lunges into their own workout programs should follow the single-leg sample progression scheme outlined in the notes below.
instructions: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand by your sides.
Step forward with one leg, lowering your body until both knees are bent at about 90 degrees.
The front knee should be aligned with your ankle, and the back knee should slightly touch, or hover just above the ground.
Push off your front foot, specifically the heel, to return to the starting position.
Alternate legs and repeat for the desired number of reps.
tips: Keep your front knee in line with your toes, not extending past them. This helps protect your joints and ensures proper form.
Keep your core tight throughout the movement to stabilize your torso and protect your lower back.
Lower yourself slowly and under control. Don’t drop into the lunge too quickly, and push back to the starting position with control.
Start with bodyweight lunges to master the movement. Once comfortable, gradually add light dumbbells, focusing on form first.
Keep in mind that with any sort of lunge or split squat pattern, if you want to emphasize the quads, focus on taking a slightly smaller step and driving up through the ball of the foot,
If you want to emphasize the glutes and hamstrings during any sort of lunge or split squat pattern, focus on taking a slightly larger step and driving up through the heel of the foot.

Forward lunges are a more advanced progression and should only be utilized once one has the requisite hip and core stability.
